svg.text: Workload archetypes — pick first, then scaffold
The contract a thin prompt inherits: one archetype decides which manifests exist and which inputs are mandatory
Maps to exactly one archetype — never two, never none
Choosing between them — three traps that look like the wrong archetype
Process loops with an internal sleep
Not a worker. Let the CronJob controller own the schedule
so failures surface as failed Jobs instead of silent sleeps.
Worker polls a queue on a timer
Scaling on queue depth is the whole reason to migrate it.
A timer poll throws that away.
Serves HTTP and consumes a queue
Unless they genuinely share in-process state — two
scaling profiles fighting over one Deployment is the smell.
The five archetypes — what each one is and what it costs you in inputs
queue URL or name per worker
Every archetype except helm-chart also gets serviceaccount.yaml and networkpolicy.yaml in base — that is why helm-chart is the escape hatch, not a default.
a half-populated tree is harder to fix than an empty one
Always required: app_name · archetype · source image (any registry or a local build)
Never scaffold with placeholders for archetype-critical fields — ask instead
The deployed image is never the source registry. Mirror into the existing project ECR repo named after the app:
111122223333.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com/<app> — do not create the ECR repository
Ask about these when relevant to any archetype
Configuration — do not rewrite a working config path
Prefer a ConfigMap for small, mostly-static configuration.
If the app already reads config from object storage (-config s3://bucket/key.json), keep that mechanism and grant GetObject — translating it is migration risk with no payoff.
Explicit CPU and memory requests and limits on every container — including init containers and sidecars.
networkpolicy.yaml with default-deny-all, then one allow per required flow (DNS always; HTTPS / Pod Identity / SSH / ingress as needed). Never combine allows into one object.
Labels per gitops-conventions: Namespace name + owner; everything else app.kubernetes.io/name + owner;
selectors and NetPol podSelector use app.kubernetes.io/name; manifests kustomization adds app.kubernetes.io/part-of.
When secrets are needed: overlay secretproviderclass.yaml in both clusters, plus CSI mount, secretKeyRef, and secretsmanager:GetSecretValue in iam.tf.
web-service only: readiness and liveness probes on every HTTP container; Deployment rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable: 0 / maxSurge: 1.
replicas (or autoscaler min) >= 2: add poddisruptionbudget.yaml with minAvailable: 1. Never on a single-replica app — it blocks drains.
Two archetypes carry extra rules the manifests alone will not teach you
Multiple worker roles sharing an image belong in a single
app, differentiated by queue env var in overlay patches.
One ScaledObject per Deployment. Share a single
Mount secrets on each Job pod directly.
No long-lived pause Deployment to keep a secret synced —
it costs a pod around the clock for nothing.
Set readOnlyRootFilesystem: true and give the job an
so completed Jobs do not accumulate.
Set concurrencyPolicy: Forbid unless overlapping runs are safe.
Every app gets apps/<app>/README.md: what it does, its inputs and outputs, its schedule or trigger, and which AWS resources it touches.
queue-worker and scheduled-job also get a small Mermaid data-flow diagram — those are the apps whose behaviour is least obvious from the manifests.
pick → choose carefully → collect inputs → scaffold → harden → document
